concept.name: Taker fee
concept.definition: The fee charged on an execution that removes liquidity - an order that executes immediately against resting interest. Under maker-taker pricing the taker pays the venue's highest per-share fee, funding the rebates paid to makers.
concept.intuition: Crossing the spread for immediacy has a price: the taker fee is the toll for not waiting.
concept.mechanics: Any order that executes on arrival - market orders, marketable limits, IOC sweeps - is the liquidity remover and is charged the removal rate (e.g., Nasdaq's $0.0030 per share for shares at or above $1). Taker status, not order type, determines the charge: a limit order that is marketable on arrival takes.
concept.formula: Taker fee = removal rate x shares executed (e.g., $0.0030/share on Nasdaq's standard tier).
concept.failure_modes: Aggressive strategies systematically pay the taker rate on every fill, and at scale the fee rivals or exceeds the spread itself - high-frequency takers can see fees consume their entire margin. Volume-tiered pricing also means the realized rate depends on month-end totals, complicating per-trade accounting.
concept.misconceptions: A limit order is not exempt from taker fees - marketability at arrival, not order type, decides maker/taker. Nor are taker fees profit for the broker: they are exchange charges, often passed through.
concept.example: You send a marketable IOC buy for 10,000 shares; as the remover you pay roughly $30 in taker fees at $0.0030 per share, while the resting sellers collect maker rebates.
